Next month the 26th marks the one-year anniversary of the Tai Po Wang Fuk Court fire. The independent committee investigating the fire is expected to submit its report to the Chief Executive before the end of October. Recent reports indicate that the government has activated the Head of Department Accountability Mechanism to investigate the administrative responsibility for the blaze, and has redeployed administrative officers to assist. Chief Executive John Lee today (the 6th) did not respond to whether the mechanism had been activated, saying only that the government had made a series of arrangements and would push forward reforms and pursue accountability as soon as possible after the report is submitted. On the Stanley luxury residence One Stanley being exposed for steel reinforcement not matching the plans, Lee said the Buildings Department is investigating the case and he has asked the Development Bureau to monitor the investigation. With multiple projects being exposed for problems one after another, he said he attaches importance to the construction quality of Hong Kong's building works, as this concerns the professionalism, quality, and safety of Hong Kong's construction, and the government will strictly enforce the law.

Nearly a year has passed since the Wang Fuk Court fire, and the independent committee is expected to submit its report before the end of October. (File photo)

Earlier media reports said that two administrative officers — former Deputy Secretary for Security Mo Kwan-yu and Commissioner for Sports Choi Kin-bun — would serve in a supporting role in the investigation小组 under the Public Service Commission, specifically responsible for preliminary work on administrative accountability.

Before attending the Executive Council meeting this morning, Chief Executive John Lee met the press. He was asked whether the reports were true, and whether activating the Head of Department Accountability Mechanism to investigate responsibility means that even with a report, if official accountability is involved there will not be immediate results — how long would the public have to wait?

Lee said he had made clear from the start that after the independent committee submits its report, he would actively study and follow up on its recommendations, carry out reforms, and announce the details. He did not give a direct answer as to whether administrative officers had already been redeployed to prepare for preliminary investigative work, saying only that "the government has made a series of arrangements during this period," and stressing that after the report is submitted, based on its contents, "comprehensive reforms will be pushed forward as soon as possible in the short term, and accountability will be pursued," with a detailed announcement to be made at that time.

Lee said that after the independent committee submits its report, reforms and accountability will be pursued as soon as possible based on the report's contents. (File photo)

Lee also reiterated on multiple occasions that improvement measures brook no delay. Hence when delivering the Policy Address in September he announced seven priority improvement measures: banning smoking at worksites, strengthening regulation of fire service installations, stepping up disciplinary action against professionals and contractors, improving compliance in owners' corporations, studying the criminalisation of bid-rigging, providing for the first time tendering and evaluation services, drawing up pre-qualification lists for consultants and contractors, and studying schemes to better assist the public in handling professional works.

According to records, the Public Service Commission is an independent statutory advisory body that advises the Chief Executive on the appointment, promotion, and discipline of civil servants. The Head of Department Accountability Mechanism was put forward by Chief Executive John Lee in last year's Policy Address, establishing a two-tier investigation mechanism based on the severity of departmental issues. Where the issue is less serious in nature or involves an isolated incident, the first-tier investigation will be conducted by the head of department. Where a department has a serious problem, or one involving extensive or repeated systemic issues, or which may implicate the role of the head of department, the second-tier investigation will be carried out by an investigation小组 led by the Public Service Commission.

The luxury residence One Stanley was exposed for having steel reinforcement in units that did not match the plans. Lee said he would not comment on cases still under investigation, and had asked the Development Bureau to oversee the Buildings Department's investigation.

One Stanley "missing rebar" — Development Bureau required to oversee investigation

Recently, one after another, construction projects have been exposed for problems, including tilting lift shafts in the new block at Queen Mary Hospital, concrete cube samples at a Tung Chung public housing estate failing to meet strength standards, and floor-slab steel reinforcement at the Stanley luxury residence One Stanley not matching the plans. Lee was asked whether there were problems in construction and even in project oversight?

Responding to the One Stanley project issue, he said the Buildings Department is seriously investigating the case, "looking into issues such as whether construction quality and supervision were adequate, and will handle it strictly in accordance with the law." As the investigation is still ongoing, he would not comment on the case, and had asked the Development Bureau to oversee the investigation. He stressed, however, that he attaches importance to the construction quality of Hong Kong's building works, "will pay attention to whether professionals related to the works have duly supervised, and whether contractors have carried out construction in violation of regulations," and said this concerns the professionalism, quality, and safety of Hong Kong's construction, and the government will definitely strictly enforce the law.

He has also asked the Development Bureau, with regard to building works as a whole, to raise regulatory requirements and penalties under the law to ensure the legislation's deterrent effect, severely punish those who violate regulations, and safeguard the professionalism, quality, and safety of Hong Kong's building works. The Development Bureau will submit proposed amendments to the Buildings Ordinance this year to strengthen regulation and enhance the disciplinary system and penalties, and the authorities will press ahead with the work at full speed.

The problem of nursing graduates finding it hard to get jobs has recently drawn attention. Lee said demand for nurses has long existed, and noted that the Hospital Authority currently has more than 3,000 nurse vacancies which graduates can apply for. (File photo)

ExCo member Tommy Cheung slams "unions putting on an act" — Lee says demand has long existed

Discussion of nurses finding it hard to get jobs has heated up recently. The trigger was a phone-in segment on a radio programme after the Policy Address, in which a Mr. Kwok, who said he was a psychiatric nurse in a disciplined service, claimed his application for deferred retirement had been rejected, and that his daughter, who studied nursing, had been unemployed immediately upon graduation, questioning the Hospital Authority's recruitment of mainland medical and nursing staff. Executive Council member Tommy Cheung subsequently questioned whether it was the unions "possibly putting on an act and making the phone calls," and said he was all in favour of importing talent from outside.

Reporters asked about the difficulty nursing graduates have finding jobs, how to address the concentration of vacancies among experienced nurses, and how to respond to remarks by Executive Council members being accused of aggravating social conflicts. Lee said that in every industry, there are situations where graduates do not immediately seek work for various individual reasons, or where recruiters pick the most suitable candidates, "and so there are cases of individuals not being hired." He stressed that society's demand for nurses has always existed, particularly as Hong Kong's healthcare continues to develop and with the trend of population ageing, "so recruitment numbers will ultimately necessarily reflect this existing demand." He also pointed out, without naming anyone, that "different discussions in society on this aspect allow everyone to discuss the issue more clearly."

Lee also pointed out that according to the 2025/26 figures, there are about 4,000 potential nursing graduates, with around 2,500 actually applying to the Hospital Authority, meaning 1,500 were applying for positions outside the Hospital Authority, while the Authority still has more than 3,000 nurse vacancies at present. "Nursing graduates can apply, and there is a chance of being hired."

Secretary for Health Professor Lo Chung-mau earlier在接受多間媒體訪問 clarified that the government's recruitment policy definitely puts local talent first. Lee also reiterated that, based on the Hospital Authority's current number of nurses, "99.8% are nurses trained locally in Hong Kong," clearly implementing the local-talent-first recruitment policy. He also pointed out that currently 40% of nurses serve in the public healthcare system, with the remaining 60% in other healthcare roles, such as community nursing, elderly care, rehabilitation services, and private medical institutions. He stressed that society's demand for nurses has long existed, and the government will, in line with healthcare service needs, exchange opinions with the trade and academia, and plan well for medical and nursing training and manpower development.
